sentences.text: Lunaspis were flat fish with elongated pectoral spines and shortened thoracic armor, possessing a body compressed dorsoventrally like other petalichthyid fish.
They had long, thin tails resembling whips, while their curved spinal plates acted as wings off the center armor featuring many small spines along their anterior ridge.
The long, spine-like plates suggest a crescent moon shape, which inspired the genus name 'moon-shield'.
Their eyes were oriented dorsally, facing upward toward the water surface.
Specimens from Australia show tubercles on the median dorsal plate that coalesce into a distinct median dorsal ridge, a feature unique to Lunaspis within the order Petalichthyida.
The species Lunaspis broilii is commonly larger than Lunaspis heroldi.
The fusion of tubercles into a ridge is a unique trait found only in Lunaspis among its relatives.
The genus Lunaspis was first described by Broili in 1929, with the species Lunaspis heroldi discovered by Ferdinand Broili in Germany that same year.
Lunaspis were marine bottom-dwelling nektonic carnivores.
Lunaspis is classified as a placoderm.
It belongs to the order Petalichthyida.
Lunaspis belongs to the family Macropetalichthyidae.

Lunaspis was originally classified in the family Acanthaspidae, but Walter Gross's 1937 findings led to its reclassification into the family Macropetalichthyidae after Acanthaspis was synonymized with it.
Lunaspis lived in shallow marine environments during the Early Devonian, between approximately 409.1 and 402.5 million years ago.
The time range for Lunaspis is the Emsian stage, from 410.62 to 399.5 million years ago.
Fossils of Lunaspis have been found in Germany, China, and Australia.
